analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare long-term care benefit covering home care and nursing homes, financed by higher payroll taxes including on high earners.
analysis.headline: Introduced with one cosponsor in November 1991, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added long-term care to Medicare: seniors and disabled people who need substantial help with everyday activities would be entitled to paid home care — aides, nursing, therapy, respite care for family caregivers, adult day care — or nursing facility care. It would pay for this with a new federal trust fund financed by raising payroll taxes from 6.2% to 6.7% and removing the cap on wages subject to the Medicare hospital insurance tax. It also included a consumer bill of rights, complaint hotlines, and inspection requirements, and let disabled people buy into Medicare during the two-year waiting period they normally face. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people who cannot perform basic daily activities without help — and their families. Medicare would pay for home and community care so people could stay in their homes instead of entering institutions, and for nursing facility care after a $500 copayment per 30 days. Severely disabled dependent children under 19 would become newly eligible, and people with disabilities could purchase Medicare coverage during the 24-month waiting period [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people needing daily care

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new Medicare Part C entitlement paying for home and community care — home health aides, nursing, therapies, medical supplies, respite care for family caregivers, and adult day care — for people certified as unable to perform at least two activities of daily living without substantial help [S2] [S3].
Also covers nursing facility care, with a $500 copayment for each 30 days of care and federal payment of $63 per day after the first 90 days [S3].
Extends eligibility to dependent children under 19 who are chronically dependent or who need a medical device plus ongoing nursing care to avoid death or serious disability [S3].

Establishes a long-term home care consumers' bill of rights, statewide toll-free complaint hotlines, state Consumer Boards and community advisory boards dominated by consumers, and sanctions including fines and license revocation for agencies that fail quality standards [S2] [S3].
Lets individuals with disabilities buy into Medicare during the 24-month waiting period they normally must serve before becoming eligible [S2] [S3].
Gives people denied coverage the same hearing and judicial review procedures that apply to Medicare hospital insurance appeals [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and employers. The bill raises the Old-Age, Survivors and Disability Insurance payroll tax from 6.2% to 6.7% for both employees and employers starting in 1993, and removes the ceiling on wages subject to the Medicare hospital insurance tax entirely — meaning high earners would pay the tax on all their earnings, not just up to the cap. Nursing facility residents bear a $500 copayment per 30 days of care, and home care agencies and case-management agencies bear the cost of complying with new training, survey, and quality requirements [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: All workers, employers, and high earners

drawbacks.text: The financing falls on payroll taxes, which are paid by every working person and their employer regardless of income, in addition to the new cap-free Medicare tax on high earners [S2] [S3].
Nursing facility residents would pay a $500 copayment for each 30 days of care — a real cost for families already facing long stays [S3].

If spending on home care exceeded the new tax revenue, the bill's self-financing mechanism would automatically impose a copayment of up to 5% of the national average daily payment rate on home care recipients to close half the gap [S2] [S3].

The bill routes all payments through home care agencies and case-management agencies and subjects them to training, supervision, survey, and sanction requirements, which the bill itself acknowledges would have economic impacts on those agencies — costs that could limit availability of services, particularly in rural areas and minority communities, which the bill requires the Secretary to monitor [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and targeted at one of the biggest financial risks families face: long-term care, which Medicare did not then and does not now cover. Home-based care with family caregiver respite is also what most families say they want, over institutional care. The cost is real but broadly shared: a half-point payroll tax increase on workers and employers, and uncapped Medicare taxes on high earners, plus copayments on nursing home care. The self-financing trigger that could impose automatic copayments if costs overrun is a design weakness, and the new entitlement would have been a major long-term commitment. On balance, this was a substantial expansion of the social safety net paid for openly rather than borrowed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day in November 1991, and the committee never took it up; the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Simon introduced the bill on November 22, 1991, together with Sen. Paul Wellstone as cosponsor [S3] [S4] [S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which handles Medicare legislation [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the bill's complete action history contains only the introduction and referral [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill expired with it [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No new long-term care benefit was created, so families facing catastrophic care costs continued to pay out of pocket or spend down their savings to qualify for Medicaid, while employers and high earners avoided the payroll tax increase that would have funded the program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and high earners avoided the tax; families kept paying

for.name: Sen. Paul Simon
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, which would have added long-term care coverage to Medicare financed by payroll taxes.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: The Senate committee to which Medicare legislation is referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 22, 1991 and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining fourteen months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators sponsored the bill and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan breakdown of support was never measured.

industries.industry: Home care and home health agencies
industries.note: The bill would have made Medicare a new payer for home aides, nursing, therapy, and adult day care, routing public money through these agencies to deliver care people want at home. It also imposed training, supervision, and survey requirements on them, with fines and license revocation for failures.

The bill created a new federal per-diem payment for nursing facility care after residents meet a $500-per-30-days copayment, giving facilities a large new source of revenue alongside Medicaid and Medicare.
Employers would have paid a payroll tax of 6.7% instead of 6.2% starting in 1993, so their interest in this bill was in its failure, which is what happened.
The bill removed the wage cap on the Medicare hospital insurance tax entirely, so high earners would have paid it on all earnings; avoiding that tax is the interest they had in the bill dying.
